new_statements.quote: Was den Akzent betrifft, dessen Besonderheiten schon Last (a. a. O., S. 4) bemerkt, so läßt sich zwar erkennen, daß von vokalisch auslautenden Wörtern alle Zweisilber und die Mehrsilber mit langem Vokal oder Diphthong der vorletzten Silbe als Paroxytona, die Mehrsilber mit kurzem Vokal in der vorletzten als Proparoxytona behandelt werden; konsonantisch auslautende Wörter werden aber ohne bisher erkennbare Regel teils auf der letzten, teils auf der vorletzten Silbe betont. Das adjektivische a- zieht immer den Hauptton auf sich. Nebentöne sind sowohl bei drei- als auch zweisilbigen Oxytonen zu beobachten.
new_statements.translation: As for the accent, whose peculiarities Last (op. cit., p. 4) already noted, one can recognise that, among vowel-final words, all disyllables and those polysyllables with a long vowel or diphthong in the penultimate syllable are treated as paroxytones, while polysyllables with a short vowel in the penult are treated as proparoxytones; consonant-final words, however, are stressed sometimes on the last, sometimes on the penultimate syllable, without any rule recognisable so far. The adjectival a- always attracts the main stress. Secondary stresses can be observed in both trisyllabic and disyllabic oxytones.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Vowel-final words: stress the penult if the word is disyllabic or if the penult has a long vowel or diphthong; otherwise (short penult in a longer word) stress the antepenult. Consonant-final words: final or penultimate stress, unpredictable. The adjectival/genitival prefix a- always carries main stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Nebentöne sind sowohl bei drei- als auch zweisilbigen Oxytonen zu beobachten' - secondary stresses observed on disyllabic and trisyllabic words with final main stress; no placement rule given.
new_statements.exceptions: Consonant-final words show final or penultimate stress with no rule the author could recognise; the adjectival a- overrides the rule by always taking main stress. Struck notes Last had already remarked on the accent's peculiarities.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, wordlist/vocabulary data of the 'Manati' (Mangati = Barabaig) dialect with parallels from the Ufiome-settled Tatoga, compiled by Struck from Werther, Kannenberg, Last, Meinhof and others' notes (pp. 111-112 explain the multi-source transcription method). Pre-phonemic 1911 description with no tone marking. All modern descriptions treat Datooga as a two-tone language (Rottland 1982: 155 lists only length and tone under 'Prosodische Erscheinungen' and says nothing about stress; Kießling 2000: 'Datooga is a tone language'; Griscom 2019: 68 on Asimjeeg: H/L, TBU = syllable, little weight sensitivity) and none gives a word-stress rule; Kießling 1998: 7 mentions a 'Druckakzent' on plural object suffixes in one paradigm only. Struck's 'Akzent' is therefore possibly a hearing of tonal prominence; final short vowels are weak/devoiced (Rottland 1982: 155; Kießling 1998 fn. 1), which is consistent with his penult/antepenult pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: Struck 1911 describes the 'Manati' (Mangati = Barabaig) dialect with Ufiome-dialect parallels, i.e. varieties inside dato1239 (Barabayiiga-Gisamjanga). Rottland 1982 §7.1 covers all six Datooga dialects (D1-D6) jointly. Kießling's papers use Gisamjanga data (Berger 1935-36, Dongobesh), also inside dato1239. Griscom 2019 describes Asimjeeg/Isimjeega, which Glottolog lists separately as tsim1256 (Griscom himself calls it 'a variety of Datooga (Glottocode: dato1239)'); its tone findings are cited here as context only.
